chapter.name: The Constitution of India: An Introduction

questions.q: True or False: In the chapter's kabaddi story the referee had already seen that the player was out, so the rulebook added nothing to how the dispute ended. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The referee's own view did not end the quarrel. She pulled out the rulebook to settle it amicably, and the dispute ended only when the team captains conferred with her, looked at the rules together and agreed that the player was out.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the captains conferred, looked at the rules and agreed, which is what settled it amicably

questions.q: Dr. Rajendra Prasad said a democratic Constitution works only if those who work with it have 'willingness to respect the viewpoint of others, capacity for compromise and accommodation'. (i) In the kabaddi story, what did the captains do after the referee pulled out the rulebook, and which words of Dr. Prasad does that match? (ii) Why would a rulebook that one captain refused to look at fail to settle the dispute?
questions.a: (i) The captains conferred with the referee and looked at the rules, then agreed that the player was out; this matches 'willingness to respect the viewpoint of others' and 'capacity for compromise and accommodation'. (ii) A rulebook settles a dispute only when all concerned accept it; if one captain would not refer to it, there would be no common text to end the argument.
s: Captains confer with the referee and look at the rules, then agree
Matched to willingness to respect others' views / compromise
A rulebook works only if all agree to refer to it

questions.q: A school council first agrees on a value, 'no student should be treated as inferior by another', and only then drafts its rules: every class elects one representative, and no senior may skip the canteen queue. Which statement about the council's method matches what the chapter says about a constitution?
o: The value is the basis from which the rules are drawn, as with a constitution's laws
The rules come first and the value is added afterwards to explain them, as the chapter describes
The value and the rules are kept apart, because a constitution's laws are drawn up without values
The value matters only for the two rules, since a constitution lays out nothing beyond its rules
questions.a: The chapter says that the values and ideals a country is committed to (equality and justice for all, fraternity, pluralism, freedom) are what usually form the basis for the laws and principles in a constitution. The council did the same: value first, rules drawn from it.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A document that only describes how the legislature, executive and judiciary are formed and what each may do would still be short of a full constitution.
Reason (R): A constitution also lays out checks and balances amongst the three organs, to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A. The chapter lists checks and balances (together with the rights and duties of citizens and the long-term goals) as something a constitution lays out in addition to the framework of the organs. A document without them would lack the part that ensures accountability.

questions.q: A match rulebook can settle whether a kabaddi player is 'out'. Name one thing a country's constitution lays out that no match rulebook could supply, and describe a situation in a citizen's life where she would need it.
questions.a: Any one of: the framework and roles of the three organs (e.g. a citizen wants to know which organ can punish a lawbreaker), checks and balances (a citizen wants an official's decision examined), the rights and duties of citizens (a citizen is treated unfairly and wants to know what she may demand), or the nation's long-term goals and aspirations. A game rulebook only settles disputes inside a match.
s: A valid item from what the chapter says a constitution lays out
A believable citizen's situation in which that item is needed

questions.q: Aarav says, 'A constitution is a rulebook for the people in government. It tells the legislature, the executive and the judiciary what to do, but it says nothing about ordinary citizens or the country's aims.' How far is he right? Answer with the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that a constitution frames the three organs and their roles and responsibilities. He is wrong to say it is silent on citizens and aims: it also lays out the rights and duties of citizens and outlines the long-term goals and aspirations of the nation.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right half: it frames the organs and their roles
The wrong half: it also lays out rights, duties and long-term goals

questions.q: Ritu's quiz card asks: 'The Constitution now has 25 parts and 12 schedules. By how many has the combined number of parts and schedules grown since it came into effect?' Which answer is correct?
questions.a: When it came into effect it had 22 parts and 8 schedules, a total of 30; today the total is 25 + 12 = 37. The growth is 7 (3 parts and 4 schedules).

questions.q: At a swearing-in, a High Court judge reads aloud that she 'promises to follow the provisions of the Constitution'. Her friend says, 'That is the same oath the President takes.' Which reply agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution, while the prime minister, the council of ministers and judges promise to follow its provisions. So the pledges are worded differently, though all uphold the Constitution.
o: Not the same: the President's oath is to preserve, protect and defend it, while judges promise to follow its provisions
The same: all high officials take one common oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the country
Not the same: judges alone pledge to the Constitution, while the President pledges only to Parliament and its members
The same: the President and judges both promise to follow its provisions, and only the prime minister swears to defend it

questions.q: Compare the kabaddi rulebook with the Constitution of India. Give two similarities and two differences, using what the chapter says a constitution lays out.
questions.a: Similarities: both are written texts that are consulted when a dispute arises; both work because the people concerned agree to follow them (captains and referee; officials who pledge to uphold the Constitution). Differences: the Constitution frames the three organs and checks and balances, which a game rulebook does not; it lays out the rights and duties of citizens; it states values and goals for a whole nation, where the rulebook only governs one sport.
s: Two similarities
Two differences using the four contents
A concluding sentence on why the Constitution is 'something like' a rulebook

questions.q: A district court cancels a rule issued by the collector's office because the rule goes against the Constitution. (a) Which two organs of government are involved here? (b) Which feature of the Constitution does this show at work?
questions.a: (a) The executive (the collector's office, which implements) and the judiciary (the court, which ensures that laws and rules made accord with the Constitution). (b) Checks and balances among the organs, which ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
s: Part (a): executive and judiciary identified with their roles
Part (b): checks and balances ensuring accountability

questions.q: A new country's constitution has one sentence: 'The Prime Minister shall govern for the good of all.' (a) Which organ of government does the sentence mention, and which two organs does it leave out? (b) Which feature of a constitution would be missing, so that nobody could question the Prime Minister's decisions?
questions.a: (a) It mentions the executive (headed by the prime minister) and leaves out the legislature and the judiciary. (b) Checks and balances among the organs, which ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
s: Part (a): executive mentioned; legislature and judiciary left out
Part (b): checks and balances, giving accountability

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's kabaddi story the referee still pulled out the rulebook even though she had herself seen that the player was out.
Reason (R): The referee pulled out the rulebook because she was unsure whether the player was out.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: the referee had seen the player was out, and still pulled out the rulebook. R is false: she did it to settle the dispute amicably, not because she was unsure; the captains then conferred and looked at the rules.

questions.q: The Lake View Housing Society's byelaws give a Management Committee the power to run repairs, an Events Committee the power to run festivals and a Complaints Panel the power to decide residents' disputes. They list each resident's rights and duties and state a goal of 'solar power for every block in ten years'. They say nothing about how the Complaints Panel may question the Management Committee. Which of the four things a constitution lays out is missing from these byelaws?
questions.a: The framework of the organs (three bodies with roles), the rights and duties, and the long-term goal are all present. What is absent is any way for one body to be held answerable to another, which is checks and balances.
o: Checks and balances among the committees
The framework and roles of the committees
The rights and duties of the residents
The long-term goals of the society

questions.q: A student sorts three items into the chapter's mind-map boxes (values and ideals of a society / political system / rights and duties of citizens): (i) fraternity, (ii) how the judiciary is made, (iii) the duty to protect the natural environment. (a) Place each item in its box. (b) Which of the three boxes, according to the chapter, usually forms the basis for the laws and principles in a constitution?
questions.a: (a) Fraternity belongs under values and ideals of a society; how the judiciary is made belongs under the political system; the duty to protect the environment belongs under rights and duties of citizens. (b) The values and ideals of a society.
s: Part (a): all three placed correctly
Part (b): values and ideals form the basis for the laws and principles

questions.q: A village fair committee has a Rules Group that frames the fair's rules and a Disputes Panel that decides whether a stallholder broke a rule. The third body its constitution still needs, to carry the rules out, matches the ___ organ of government.
questions.a: executive

questions.q:
Read the statements about what a constitution lays out.
1. Checks and balances among the organs of government are meant to ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
2. A constitution's values and ideals are separate from its laws; the laws are drawn up without reference to those values.
3. The Indian Constitution lays out the rights of citizens, while their duties are left to be taught by families and schools.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 1 is from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the values and ideals usually form the basis for the laws and principles in a constitution. Statement 3 is false: the Constitution lays out the rights and the duties of citizens, and Fundamental Duties are part of it.
o: 1 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
The Kolhapur District Sports Association is drafting a Charter and can keep only three of these four clauses.
Clause 1: A Selection Panel picks teams, a Games Committee runs tournaments and a Grievance Tribunal decides complaints.
Clause 2: The Tribunal may call for the Games Committee's file and ask it to explain any decision.
Clause 3: Every registered player may enter district meets; every player must report an injury within a day.
Clause 4: By 2035 there will be a coaching academy in each taluka.
Member X wants to drop Clause 2: the Games Committee has promised to share its files whenever asked. Member Y wants to drop Clause 4: the Association's yearly vision note can carry the academy goal, but a rival group warns that a goal left out of the Charter 'can be quietly dropped by the next committee'.
(a) Name the part of a constitution that each of Clauses 1, 2 and 4 matches.
(b) Clause 3 holds two kinds of provisions. Name them.
(c) Whose proposal should the meeting accept? Choose, and name what the Charter loses under your choice, using what the chapter says a constitution lays out.
questions.a: (a) Clause 1 is the framework of the organs and their roles; Clause 2 is checks and balances; Clause 4 is a long-term goal. (b) Rights (to enter meets) and duties (to report an injury). (c) Either side can be argued from the chapter. Dropping Clause 2 loses checks and balances, which the chapter says ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability; a promise to share files is not a provision anyone can insist on. Dropping Clause 4 loses a long-term goal, which the chapter also counts among the things a constitution lays out, and the goal then depends on a note that is not binding. Full marks need a named loss from the chapter and a reason why that loss is the smaller one.
s: Part (a): organs, checks and balances, long-term goals matched
Part (b): rights and duties
Part (c): a choice with the loss named from the chapter (1) and a reason why it is the smaller loss (1)

questions.q:
At a district kho-kho final in Hyderabad the scores were level. A chaser claimed she had tagged a runner before the runner crossed the line; the runner's team disagreed. The referee opened the official rulebook, and both captains read the page and agreed on the result. The sports officer now wants one plan for the 16-team knockout (15 matches) that follows. Plan P: both captains sign, before each first whistle, that they accept the rulebook; signing takes 5 minutes a match, and the day's schedule has only 60 minutes of spare time. Plan Q: each captain gets a short rule card at the toss, and the full rulebook stays with the referee, to be shown only if a dispute arises.
(a) Which plan matches the way the referee used the rulebook in the final, and which matches the way the President, the prime minister, the ministers and the judges treat the Constitution? What does the chapter say each of these officials does?
(b) How many minutes does Plan P add over the 15 matches, and by how many minutes does it overshoot the spare time?
(c) The officer can adopt only one plan. Choose one. Then state the objection to your choice that you find hardest to answer, and say whether the chapter's question about captains who do not agree to refer to the rulebook at all helps you answer it.
questions.a: (a) Plan Q matches the referee (the rulebook comes out when a dispute arises); Plan P matches the officials, who pledge in advance. The President takes an oath to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution; the prime minister, council of ministers and judges promise to follow its provisions. (b) 15 x 5 = 75 minutes; 75 - 60 = 15 minutes over. (c) Either plan can be defended. For P: a rulebook settles a dispute only if all concerned agree to refer to it, and advance agreement, like the officials' pledge, secures that, at a cost of 15 minutes. For Q: it fits the schedule, and its hardest objection is the captain who never agreed to the rules and refuses to look at them in the quarrel; the chapter's question about captains who do not agree to refer to the rulebook shows why that objection is serious and cannot be fully answered. Marks go for naming the objection and testing it against the chapter.
s: Part (a): Q for the referee, P for the officials, with the oath and the promise
Part (b): 75 minutes and 15 minutes over
Part (c): a decision (1) with the hardest objection named and tested against the chapter (1)

questions.q: A friend argues, 'A country does not need a written constitution; honest leaders and a fair judge are enough.' Argue against her using four things the chapter says a constitution lays out, and the pledge officials take.
questions.a: A written constitution frames the three organs and their roles, so no leader has to guess his power. It sets checks and balances so that fairness, responsibility and accountability do not depend on one leader's honesty. It lays out the rights and duties of citizens, so people know what they may demand. It outlines long-term goals the nation shares beyond any leader. Officials pledge to uphold it, which makes their honesty accountable to a text everyone has accepted, as the captains accepted the rulebook.
s: Organs and roles written down
Checks and balances instead of reliance on honesty
Rights and duties of citizens
Long-term goals of the nation
Pledge to uphold it, like the agreed rulebook

questions.q: Write a short situation from school life in which a written rulebook settles an argument. Then say which part of a country's constitution your rulebook is most like and why.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. two classes dispute a tie in a quiz and the written quiz rules decide it. The rulebook is like the part of the Constitution that sets rules and checks and balances, since both settle disputes by a text everyone accepted earlier.
s: A believable situation where a written rule settles the argument
Names a matching part of the Constitution (organs, checks and balances, rights and duties or goals)
Reason linking the two

questions.q: Write a quiz question about the Constituent Assembly whose correct answer is 90 members. Then name one wrong answer that a careless student could give, and the slip that would lead to it.
questions.a: The Assembly began with 389 members and was reduced to 299 after the Partition of India, so the fall was 389 - 299 = 90. Question e.g. 'By how many members did the Partition reduce the Constituent Assembly?' A wrong answer: 23 (the percentage fall, 90/389, given instead of the number) or 299 (stating the later size instead of the difference).
s: A question that uses 389 and 299 and has 90 as its answer
A plausible wrong answer
The slip explained correctly

questions.q: Three school questions are put beside the chapter's list of what India's leaders had to decide: (i) 'Which languages will our assemblies use?' (ii) 'Who may vote in school elections?' (iii) 'How will we settle a quarrel between two clubs?' Which of them matches a question the chapter lists, and which does not appear in the chapter's list?
questions.a: (ii) matches 'Who should have the right to vote?' and (iii) matches 'How should we decide on disputes?'. (i) is not among the questions the chapter lists (type of government, rules and principles, right to vote, deciding disputes).
s: (ii) and (iii) matched with the chapter's questions
(i) identified as not in the chapter's list

questions.q: A quiz answer sheet reads: (i) 'Chairman of the Drafting Committee: Dr. Rajendra Prasad.' (ii) 'President of the Constituent Assembly at the start of the writing of the Constitution: Dr. Sachidananda Sinha.' (iii) 'First Law and Justice minister of independent India: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.' One entry is wrong. Find it, correct it, and say what the person you named in the correction was chairman of.
questions.a: Entry (i) is wrong. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee that prepared the initial text. Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly as a whole. Entries (ii) and (iii) agree with the chapter.
s: Entry (i) identified as the wrong one, corrected to Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
Dr. Rajendra Prasad: Chairman of the whole Constituent Assembly

questions.q: A quiz card says: 'Fifteen of the Constituent Assembly's members were women, exactly 10 per cent of its members.' Using the numbers in the chapter, show that this cannot be true whether the Assembly is counted at its original size or after the Partition.
questions.a: The Assembly began with 389 members and was later reduced to 299. 15/389 x 100 = 3.9 per cent (to one decimal place) and 15/299 x 100 = 5.0 per cent. Neither is 10 per cent; 10 per cent of 389 would be about 39 women and of 299 about 30.
s: Uses both sizes, 389 and 299
15/389 about 3.9 per cent and 15/299 about 5.0 per cent
Concludes that neither equals 10 per cent

questions.q: The chapter says planning how India would govern itself had to begin 'while India was struggling for independence'. (a) Give two of the questions it lists that the planners had to answer. (b) Pick one of them and say, using the chapter's description of India, why it was hard to answer.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: what type of government we should have; what rules and principles should guide us; who should have the right to vote; how we should decide on disputes. (b) For example, 'who should have the right to vote' was hard because India is a large, culturally diverse and complex country, so one answer had to suit people of many regions and social groups.
s: Two of the listed questions
One question linked to India being large, culturally diverse and complex

questions.q: Dr. Sachidananda Sinha hoped the Assembly's proceedings would be marked by 'good sense, public spirit, and genuine patriotism, but also by wisdom, toleration, justice, and fairness to all'. The Assembly had to answer four questions: what type of government to have, what rules and principles should guide the country, who should have the right to vote, and how disputes should be decided. Pair three different qualities from his list with three of these questions and explain in one line why each quality is needed for that question. Then say which question would most test the quality of toleration in an Assembly of members from diverse regions and social groups, and why.
questions.a: Any three sensible pairs, e.g. fairness to all with 'who should vote' (no group should be left out), justice with 'how to decide disputes' (a quarrel must be judged fairly), wisdom with 'what rules and principles should guide us' (choices affect the whole country). Toleration is most tested by 'what type of government' or 'who should vote', since members from different regions and groups would hold different views and each had to accept those unlike their own.
s: First pair with a reason
Second pair with a reason
Third pair with a reason
A question chosen for toleration
Reason linked to the Assembly's diversity of regions and groups

questions.q: A school stages a mock Constituent Assembly with 40 seats and wants it to be like the real Assembly in the way the chapter describes its members. Which seat plan does that?
questions.a: The chapter says the members represented India's diverse regions, professions and social groups. A plan that spreads seats across classes, genders and interest groups copies that. The other plans pick one group, which the chapter does not describe.
o: Seats shared among students from every class, both genders and different interest groups such as sports, music and science clubs
All 40 seats to the 40 students with the highest marks, since the real Assembly was a gathering of the best scholars
All 40 seats to the elected class monitors, since the real Assembly was made up of one chosen group of leaders
All 40 seats to the oldest class, since the real Assembly was formed by the senior-most members of society

questions.q: Trace the making of the Constitution from the formation of the Assembly to Republic Day. Give the date of each stage, work out how long the Assembly's work took and how long the Constitution waited before coming into effect, and explain what Republic Day celebrates.
questions.a: The Assembly was formed on 9 December 1946 with members elected by the provincial legislative assemblies. A Drafting Committee prepared the initial text, and the Assembly developed and wrote the Constitution. It was adopted on 26 November 1949, 1,083 days after formation, which is almost three years. It came into effect on 26 January 1950, 61 days after adoption. Republic Day celebrates the coming into effect of the Constitution.
s: Formation date and how the members were chosen
Drafting Committee's initial text and the Assembly's writing
Adoption date and 1,083 days (almost three years)
Effect date and 61 days after adoption
Republic Day celebrates the coming into effect

questions.q:
A school's mock Assembly mirrors the real one. Match each mock event (Column A) with the part of the real process it copies (Column B).
Column A: 1. Class councils elect the members of the mock Assembly.  2. A three-student team writes the first draft of the mock rules.  3. The head girl presides over all the sittings of the mock Assembly.  4. The principal announces the day on which the finished rules begin to apply.
Column B: a. The Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar  b. The Chairman, Dr. Rajendra Prasad  c. The legislative assemblies of the provinces  d. The coming into effect on 26 January 1950
questions.a: Class councils elected the members, as the provincial legislative assemblies did; the three-student team copies the Drafting Committee that prepared the initial text; the head girl presiding copies the Chairman of the whole Assembly; the day the rules begin to apply copies the coming into effect on 26 January 1950.

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Constituent Assembly.
1. It was formed in 1946 with 299 members, a number later increased to 389 after the Partition of India.
2. Its members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had in turn been elected by the people.
3. The Drafting Committee that prepared the initial text was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the first Law and Justice minister of independent India.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 1 swaps the numbers: the Assembly began with 389 members and was later reduced to 299 after the Partition.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: The Partition of India cut the Constituent Assembly from 389 members to 299, a fall of about ___ per cent (to the nearest whole number).

A Delhi school's Republic Day play on the making of the Constitution has four scene cards: Card 1, the Assembly's first meeting (9 December 1946); Card 2, the Drafting Committee at work; Card 3, the Constitution's adoption (26 November 1949); Card 4, the Constitution's coming into effect (26 January 1950). The play must be cut to three cards, and the teacher says the audience must still be able to answer the chapter's question 'How was the Indian Constitution prepared?'
(a) Who chaired the Drafting Committee of Card 2, and who chaired the Assembly of Card 1?
(b) The chapter says the real Assembly was formed in 1946 with a larger number of members that was later reduced to 299 after the Partition. By what percentage did its membership fall? Give it to one decimal place.
(c) Which card should be cut? Choose, and say what the audience will no longer be able to work out for itself.
questions.a: (a) Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly. (b) The Assembly began with 389 members and fell to 299, a loss of 90; 90/389 x 100 = 23.1 per cent. (c) Any card can be defended if the loss is named. Cutting Card 4 leaves the audience without the date that Republic Day marks, though the Assembly's work was done by then; cutting Card 2 removes the Drafting Committee's initial text, though the Assembly still developed and wrote the Constitution; cutting Card 1 removes how long the work took and who the members were; cutting Card 3 removes the date the document was adopted. Marks go for a named loss that follows from the chapter.
s: Part (a): Ambedkar for the Drafting Committee, Prasad for the Assembly
Part (b): 389 to 299 from the chapter, 23.1 per cent
Part (c): a card chosen (1), with the loss named from the chapter (1)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Constitution of India was in force from the day the Constituent Assembly adopted it.
Reason (R): Republic Day, observed each 26 January, marks the coming into effect of the Constitution.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false: the Assembly adopted the Constitution on 26 November 1949 and it came into effect later, on 26 January 1950. R is true as the chapter states it, and in fact shows why A is wrong.

questions.q: True or False: The Constituent Assembly's work was over once the Drafting Committee had prepared the initial text. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The Drafting Committee prepared only the initial text. The Constituent Assembly developed and wrote the Constitution over almost three years and adopted it on 26 November 1949.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the Assembly developed and wrote the document and adopted it later; the Committee prepared the initial text

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Constituent Assembly was reduced by 90 members after the Partition of India.
Reason (R): Its members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces, whose members had in turn been elected by the people.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. The fall from 389 to 299 followed the Partition of India; how the members were elected is a separate fact about the Assembly and says nothing about why its size fell.

questions.q: Meera says, 'From the day the Constituent Assembly was formed to the day the Constitution came into effect, more than three years passed; but the Assembly's own work of writing and adopting it took a little less than three years.' Check her claim with the chapter's dates.
questions.a: Meera is right. 9 December 1946 to 26 January 1950 is 1,144 days, more than three years (1,096 days). The Assembly's work, from 9 December 1946 to adoption on 26 November 1949, took 1,083 days, 13 days short of three years.
s: Verdict: right
Formation to effect: 1,144 days, more than 1,096
Formation to adoption: 1,083 days, less than 1,096

questions.q:
Nagpur's Kendriya Vidyalaya plans a Mock Constituent Assembly of 60 students for Republic Day week. The principal wants every class to be heard and the Assembly to finish its work within the week. Plan A: every student votes directly for all 60 members in one day; the counting takes a full day, and with 12 classes it is possible that a class gets no member at all. Plan B: each of the 12 class councils (elected by their classmates) elects 5 members; this takes three days. During the week, 6 of the 60 members must leave for a sports meet.
(a) How many members does Plan B choose in all, and what proportion of the 60 remains after the 6 leave?
(b) The chapter says the real Assembly began with 389 members and was later reduced to 299 after the Partition. If the 60-member mock Assembly shrank by the same proportion, how many members would remain, to the nearest whole number?
(c) Write your recommendation to the principal in one sentence. Then name the risk it leaves unsolved, and say whether the real Assembly's way of choosing members from the chapter reduces that risk.
questions.a: (a) 12 x 5 = 60 members; 54 remain, which is 90 per cent. (b) 60 x 299/389 = 46.1, so 46 members would remain. (c) Either plan can be defended. Plan B guarantees every class a voice and copies the real two-step process (people elected the provincial legislative assemblies, which elected the members), but it uses three days of the week. Plan A is faster but cannot guarantee that every class is heard. The answer must name the risk left (time lost under B; a class left out under A) and test it against the chapter's account of the Assembly.
s: Part (a): 60 members and 90 per cent remain
Part (b): 389 and 299 from the chapter, 46 members
Part (c): a recommendation (1), with the risk named and tested against the real Assembly's process (1)

questions.q: A mock Assembly begins with 40 members and loses the same share of its members as the real Constituent Assembly did at the Partition (389 members down to 299). About how many members does it have left? (Use the loss as a whole-number percentage.)
questions.a: The real loss was 90/389, about 23 per cent. Losing 23 per cent of 40 is about 9, so about 31 remain (299/389 of 40 is 30.7). The option 9 is the number lost, and 23 is the percentage itself.

questions.q: A student's timeline card on the Constituent Assembly has four entries. Which one entry is wrong according to the chapter?
o: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the whole Constituent Assembly.
The Assembly was formed on 9 December 1946 with 389 members.
Its members were elected by the legislative assemblies of the provinces.
A Drafting Committee prepared the initial text of the Constitution.
questions.a: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Chairman of the Constituent Assembly. The other three entries are as the chapter states.

questions.q: (a) Write the chain through which the people of India were linked to the members of the Constituent Assembly. (b) How does this differ from every adult citizen voting for each Assembly member?
questions.a: (a) The people elected the members of the provincial legislative assemblies, and these assemblies elected the Constituent Assembly's members. (b) The people did not vote for Assembly members themselves; the provincial legislators did so on their behalf.
s: Part (a): people, then provincial legislative assemblies, then Assembly members
Part (b): the legislators voted, so the people did not choose each member directly

questions.q: Rhea says, 'The makers of our Constitution studied the constitutions of other countries only because they were unsure of India's own traditions; and the idea of the Directive Principles came from Ireland.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The Directive Principles were indeed inspired by the Irish Constitution. But the chapter does not give lack of confidence as the reason: the makers studied France, the USA, the UK, Ireland, Australia and others in the Indian spirit of 'let noble thoughts come to me from every side', to explore their usefulness for India's context, while the freedom struggle and India's civilisational heritage were also influences.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right half: Directive Principles from Ireland
The wrong half: studied to explore usefulness in the spirit of 'noble thoughts from every side', not out of doubt about India's traditions

questions.q:
A Class 7 debate team in Bhubaneswar has four cards for the motion 'Most ideas in our Constitution came from abroad'.
Card 1: Every adult citizen may vote.
Card 2: Citizens have a duty to protect the natural environment.
Card 3: The government is given goals such as a good standard of living, but a court cannot force it to meet them.
Card 4: Judges decide cases free of pressure from the other organs.
(a) For Cards 1 and 2, name the source the chapter would give.
(b) For Cards 3 and 4, name the country that inspired the idea. How many of the four cards come from abroad?
(c) The judges ask the team to speak for or against the motion using only these cards. Which side must the team take? Justify with your counts and the chapter's three sources.
questions.a: (a) Card 1: experience of the freedom struggle; Card 2: India's civilisational heritage (emphasis on duties, Nature as sacred). (b) Card 3: Ireland (Directive Principles); Card 4: the USA (independent judiciary). Two of four cards come from abroad. (c) Against the motion. Two of four is exactly half, which is not 'most'; the other two cards come from the freedom struggle and the heritage, two of the chapter's three sources, and the makers studied other constitutions only to see what was useful. A team that argues for the motion must show how two of four can be called 'most'; the counts do not support it.
s: Part (a): freedom struggle for Card 1; heritage for Card 2
Part (b): Ireland for Card 3, USA for Card 4, and the count of two
Part (c): against the motion, because two of four is not most, with the chapter's three sources

questions.q: A student's poster says the ideals of 'liberty, equality, fraternity' in India's Constitution were adopted from France's constitution, which enshrined them from the French Revolution. Counting from the year of the Revolution that the chapter names to the year the Indian Constitution came into effect, those ideals had been in public view for ___ years.

The chapter says the makers studied the constitutions of several countries 'to explore their usefulness for our context'. A student argues, 'So India should have copied the UK's and Australia's ideas in full as well.' (i) What does the phrase 'usefulness for our context' tell you about how the makers treated foreign ideas? (ii) Name two ideas, each with the country, that the chapter says India took from abroad. (iii) Why does the chapter's evidence not support the student's argument about the UK and Australia?
questions.a: (i) The makers examined foreign constitutions to see what would be useful for India and took only that, in the spirit of 'let noble thoughts come to me from every side'. (ii) Any two of: liberty, equality and fraternity from France; Directive Principles from Ireland; an independent judiciary from the American Constitution. (iii) The chapter names no specific idea taken from the UK or Australia, and it says only that these were studied.
s: Foreign ideas were examined for usefulness, not copied in full
Two ideas each with the right country
No idea is named from the UK or Australia, so nothing shows copying

questions.q: A student's note reads: 'vasudhaiva kutumbakam means "let noble thoughts come to me from every side"; sarve bhavantu sukhinah means "the world is one family".' (a) The two meanings have been swapped; write each correctly. (b) Which of the chapter's two sayings explains why the makers studied other countries' constitutions?
questions.a: (a) vasudhaiva kutumbakam means 'the world is one family'; sarve bhavantu sukhinah is an invocation for the well-being of all creatures. (b) 'ā no bhadrāh kratavo yantu viśhwatah' ('Let noble thoughts come to me from every side'); neither saying in the student's note is the one the chapter uses for the makers' studying.
s: Part (a): both meanings corrected
Part (b): the 'noble thoughts from every side' saying

questions.q: A student writes, 'The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity reached India only through France; the freedom struggle never spoke of them.' Which fact in the chapter most directly contradicts her?
questions.a: The chapter lists equality of all, justice for all, freedom and fraternity among the ideals of the Indian freedom struggle that were enshrined in the Constitution. The other facts are true but do not show the freedom struggle holding these ideals.
o: The freedom struggle's ideals included equality, justice, freedom and fraternity
The French Declaration of 1789 focused on equality, liberty and justice for all
The Directive Principles of State Policy were inspired by the Irish Constitution
An independent judiciary was shaped with the help of the American Constitution

questions.q:
Read the statements about the influences on the Constitution.
1. The experience of the freedom struggle helped answer questions such as how the powers of the executive, the legislature and the judiciary are kept separate.
2. The idea of the Directive Principles of State Policy was taken from the American Constitution.
3. Respect for women and the saying sarve bhavantu sukhinah are among the principles of India's culture that find a place in the Constitution, though expressed a little differently.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the Directive Principles were inspired by the Irish Constitution; the American Constitution helped shape the concept of an independent judiciary.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The makers of the Constitution studied the constitutions of France, USA, UK, Ireland, Australia and other democratic countries.
Reason (R): The Indian tradition says 'Let noble thoughts come to me from every side'.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and the chapter itself gives R as the tradition in whose spirit the makers studied other constitutions, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A school's constitution committee has four jobs. Which job draws on the freedom struggle's experience, in the way the chapter says India's makers answered the question for the Constitution (and not on a foreign model or India's heritage)?
o: Deciding how the school's rules may be changed in future
Adding a goals page that the principal is not bound to carry out in court
Writing a duties section that every student must follow
Copying a good rule from another school's rulebook after studying it
questions.a: How the Constitution may be amended is one of the 'how' and 'what' questions answered by the experience of the freedom struggle. A goals page that cannot be enforced reflects the Directive Principles (Ireland); a duties section reflects India's heritage; copying a rule after studying another rulebook reflects the makers' study of other countries' constitutions.

questions.q: The answer to a quiz question is 'France, 1789'. Write a question that has this answer and explain in two lines how the answer is linked to the Indian Constitution.
questions.a: Example: 'Where and when did the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen come from?' The ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity in India's Constitution were adopted from France's constitution, which enshrined them from the French Revolution of 1789.
s: A suitable question with this answer
Names the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity
Link: adopted from France's constitution into India's

questions.q: Four clauses are proposed: (i) the legislature may not tell a court how to decide a case; (ii) the State shall work to give everyone a good standard of living, though no court can force it; (iii) all citizens enjoy liberty, equality and fraternity; (iv) every citizen has a duty to protect the natural environment. (a) Name the country the chapter gives as the source of the idea in (i) and in (ii). (b) Clause (iii) has two sources in the chapter and clause (iv) has an Indian one. Name them.
questions.a: (a) (i) the USA (an independent judiciary); (ii) Ireland (Directive Principles). (b) Clause (iii): the French constitution (which enshrined these ideals from the French Revolution of 1789) and the ideals of the Indian freedom struggle. Clause (iv): India's civilisational heritage (Fundamental Duties; Nature as sacred).
s: Part (a): USA for (i), Ireland for (ii)
Part (b): France and the freedom struggle for (iii); heritage for (iv)

questions.q: 'The makers of the Constitution were open to learning from the world but did not give up their own roots.' Justify this using the chapter.
questions.a: They followed the tradition of 'let noble thoughts come to me from every side' and studied the constitutions of France, USA, UK, Ireland and Australia, taking liberty, equality and fraternity, Directive Principles and an independent judiciary. Yet the freedom struggle and India's heritage (Fundamental Duties, respect for women, unity of India) remained the base.
s: States the tradition of openness to ideas from every side
Names the countries studied
Two ideas that came from abroad
Two ideas that came from India's own experience and heritage

questions.q: A student claims, 'The chapter names a specific idea that India took from each of the five countries France, the USA, the UK, Ireland and Australia.' (a) Test the claim: for which of the five does it name an idea, and for which does it not? (b) What reason does the chapter give for studying all of them?
questions.a: (a) The claim is wrong. It names an idea for France (liberty, equality, fraternity), Ireland (Directive Principles) and the USA (independent judiciary), and none for the UK or Australia. (b) To explore their usefulness for India's context, in the Indian spirit of 'let noble thoughts come to me from every side'.
s: Part (a): France, Ireland and the USA have ideas; the UK and Australia have none named
Part (b): to explore usefulness for India's context

questions.q: True or False: Because India's own traditions put great emphasis on the duties and role of the people in governance, the makers had no reason to study any other country's constitution. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The makers studied the constitutions of France, the USA, the UK, Ireland, Australia and other democratic countries, in the Indian spirit of 'let noble thoughts come to me from every side', and took ideas such as liberty, equality, fraternity, the Directive Principles and an independent judiciary. Heritage supplied some ideas (such as Fundamental Duties); it did not replace the study of others.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: they studied other constitutions in the spirit of noble thoughts from every side and took useful ideas, alongside heritage

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's Constitution adopted the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity from the French constitution.
Reason (R): Equality of all, justice for all, freedom and fraternity were also ideals of the Indian freedom struggle.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the Indian freedom struggle's ideals do not explain why the French constitution is the source of these ideals; they are a second influence, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A school drafts a charter with three lines: (i) 'Every student's opinion is heard, even when others disagree.' (ii) 'The school shall protect its trees and garden as something precious.' (iii) 'Every student shall wear the school uniform on Mondays.' Which two lines reflect principles that the chapter says are embedded in India's culture, and which principle does each reflect? Which line has no match in the chapter's list?
questions.a: Line (i) reflects the acceptance of the idea that people could have different points of view; line (ii) reflects Nature as sacred. Line (iii) has no match in the chapter's list of cultural principles (different points of view, Nature as sacred, pursuit of learning and knowledge, respect for women, vasudhaiva kutumbakam, sarve bhavantu sukhinah).
s: Lines (i) and (ii) matched to the right principles
Line (iii) identified as having no match

questions.q: A village panchayat's charter has two clauses. Clause X lists goals such as clean drinking water for every family, which no villager can force the panchayat to meet through a judge. Clause Y says the committee that hears complaints must decide free of pressure from the sarpanch. Which pair of sources does the chapter give for the ideas behind X and Y?
questions.a: Goals that a court cannot enforce are Directive Principles, an idea inspired by the Irish Constitution; a judiciary free from the other organs is the concept the American Constitution helped shape.
o: X from the Irish Constitution, Y from the American Constitution
X from the American Constitution, Y from the Irish Constitution
X from the French Constitution, Y from the Irish Constitution
X from the Irish Constitution, Y from the French Constitution

questions.q: Compare the Indian freedom movement and other countries' constitutions as influences on the Constitution. Say what kind of thing each supplied, with examples, and explain why the makers needed both.
questions.a: The freedom movement supplied ideals and experience: equality of all, justice for all, freedom, fraternity, the idea of the Constitution as a tool for achieving them, and leaders who sat in the Assembly and answered 'how' questions (every adult's vote, separation of powers, fundamental rights, amending the Constitution, Centre-State relations). Other constitutions supplied working models: liberty, equality and fraternity from France, Directive Principles from Ireland, an independent judiciary from the USA. Ideals alone do not say how government should be arranged, and models alone do not say what a nation stands for, so the makers used both.
s: Freedom movement: ideals and experience with two examples
Other constitutions: models with two examples
Why both were needed

questions.q: Four students each pair an idea of the Constitution with its source. Neel: the way every adult citizen gets the vote, from the experience of the freedom struggle. Pia: Fundamental Duties, from the Irish Constitution. Sam: respect for women, from India's civilisational heritage. Tina: an independent judiciary, from the American Constitution. Whose pairing does NOT agree with the chapter?
questions.a: Fundamental Duties come from India's civilisational heritage, which put great emphasis on the duties and role of the people in governance. The Irish Constitution inspired the Directive Principles. The other three pairings are as the chapter gives them.
o: Pia
Neel
Sam
Tina

questions.q:
Arjun in Kochi is building a wall exhibit called 'Where our Constitution's ideas came from'. The wall has room for three of five panels, and his teacher insists that all three of the chapter's sources of influence must be visible.
Panel A: Fundamental Duties.
Panel B: Directive Principles, goals that no court can force the government to meet.
Panel C: every adult citizen's right to vote.
Panel D: the principle in Indian culture that Nature is sacred.
Panel E: an independent judiciary.
(a) Name the source of influence the chapter would give for each of the five panels.
(b) How many different sets of three panels would show all three sources?
(c) Pick one such set. For each of the two sources that had two candidate panels, say what the panel you left out would have added to the exhibit.
questions.a: (a) A: India's civilisational heritage (emphasis on duties); B: the Irish Constitution; C: the experience of the freedom struggle; D: India's civilisational heritage (Nature as sacred); E: the American Constitution. (b) Heritage has two panels (A, D), the other two countries' influence has two (B, E) and the freedom struggle has one (C), so 2 x 2 x 1 = 4 sets. (c) Any of the four sets, with a reasoned remark for each rejected panel. For example, choosing A, B and C leaves out D (which would have shown a principle of Indian culture, Nature as sacred, that the chapter lists among those finding a place in the Constitution) and E (which would have shown that the makers took the concept of an independent judiciary from the American Constitution). Marks go for a valid set and for what each omitted panel would have shown, taken from the chapter.
s: Part (a): all five panels matched to their sources
Part (b): 4 sets
Part (c): a valid set (1), with what each of the two omitted panels would have added (1)

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Article 48-A makes the government responsible for protecting the environment, so a Class 7 student has no duty about it.' Mina says, 'The Constitution also asks every citizen to protect the natural environment.' Who is right according to the chapter?
questions.a: Article 48-A on environment and wildlife protection is a Directive Principle that guides the government, and one of the Fundamental Duties is to protect and improve the natural environment, including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife. Citizens have a duty even though the government has a goal.
o: Mina: Article 48-A guides the government, and a duty also asks every citizen to protect it
Rohan: Article 48-A is a Fundamental Right, so a court takes over the duty of protecting the environment
Mina: Article 48-A is a Fundamental Duty, so the government itself has no responsibility for it
Rohan: Directive Principles bind only the citizens, and the government is free to leave them out

questions.q:
A Gram Sabha in a Bihar village received four letters.
Letter 1: A man says he sees no reason to respect the national flag and the national anthem.
Letter 2: Many families say they do not get enough nutrition and ask the government to improve it.
Letter 3: A landlord refused to rent a room to a family of five because of their caste.
Letter 4: The village school has refused admission this year to 12 girls aged between nine and eleven, saying it keeps its places for boys.
The Gram Sabha has funds to support only one court case this year.
(a) Label each letter as a Fundamental Right, a Fundamental Duty or a Directive Principle.
(b) For which letters can the chapter say a judge will help, and what can the villagers do about Letter 2?
(c) Which of the letters you named in (b) should the Gram Sabha take to court this year? Choose, name the fact in the chapter you relied on, and say what the family or girls of the other letter must do meanwhile.
questions.a: (a) Letter 1: Fundamental Duty (respecting the national flag and anthem); Letter 2: Directive Principle (Article 47); Letter 3: Fundamental Right to equality; Letter 4: Fundamental Right (Article 21-A, right to education, and equality). (b) Letters 3 and 4: Fundamental Rights are promises that can be demanded from a judge when someone is treated unfairly because of who she is. Letter 2 is a goal for the government, and the villagers cannot ask a judge to force it; they can only press the government to make efforts. (c) Either letter can be defended. Letter 3 is a clear case of unfair treatment because of who the family is (caste), under the Right to Equality. Letter 4 affects 12 girls, all within the six-to-fourteen years the chapter names for education, and their right to education (Article 21-A) is denied. Full marks need a choice tied to the chapter's account of Fundamental Rights and a sensible plan for the other letter.
s: Part (a): all four letters labelled correctly
Part (b): Letters 3 and 4 enforceable by a judge; Letter 2 only a goal the government is pressed on
Part (c): a decision (1) tied to a fact in the chapter, with a plan for the other letter (1)

questions.q: Mayor Kavita proposes that the legislature itself should decide whether its own laws follow the Constitution. Show, using the chapter's idea of organs of government, why this arrangement cannot work well.
questions.a: The chapter gives this job to the judiciary, which ensures that laws made are in accordance with the Constitution. The legislature makes laws, and separation of powers is essential to effective working; if one organ made and checked its own laws, checks and balances would be lost.
s: States that the judiciary ensures laws accord with the Constitution
States that the legislature makes laws and powers must be separate
Concludes that checking its own laws removes the check

questions.q: In one village, Anil wants to go to court to make the government feed its undernourished children today, citing Article 47. In the same village, Rina's daughter is refused a place in school only because of her caste, and Rina wants to go to court. Which reply fits the chapter?
o: A judge can be asked to help Rina; Anil's matter is a Directive Principle, which a judge cannot enforce
A judge can be asked to help both Anil and Rina, since both of them cite an Article of the Constitution
A judge can be asked to help Anil; Rina's matter is a Directive Principle that only guides the government
A judge can be asked to help neither of them, because both matters are goals for the government to reach
questions.a: Rina's complaint is of unfair treatment because of who her daughter is, which is a matter of Fundamental Rights, promises that must be kept, so a judge can help. Anil's demand rests on Article 47 (nutrition and public health), a Directive Principle; if the government does not make efforts, one cannot go to a judge and complain.

questions.q: Parliament passes a law banning single-use plastic bags. The district collector's office enforces it. A shopkeeper goes to the High Court and says one clause goes against the Constitution. Describe what each organ of government does in this story, explain what 'separation of powers' protects, and say which feature of the Constitution the shopkeeper's challenge shows.
questions.a: Parliament, the legislature, makes the law. The district collector's office is part of the executive, which implements the law (at the national level the executive is headed by the prime minister). The court, the judiciary, ensures that laws made are in accordance with the Constitution and decides whether a law has been broken. Separation of powers is essential to their effective working, since no one organ both makes and judges its own acts. The challenge shows checks and balances, which ensure fairness, responsibility and accountability.
s: Legislature makes the law
Executive implements it
Judiciary tests it against the Constitution
Separation of powers explained
Checks and balances named for the challenge

questions.q: Neha says, 'The legislature makes the laws and the executive, headed by the prime minister, carries them out, so the judiciary only decides punishments for people who break the law.' How far is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. The legislature does make the laws and the executive, headed by the prime minister, implements them, and the judiciary does decide whether a law has been broken and the punishment. But 'only' is wrong: the judiciary also ensures that all laws made are in accordance with the Constitution.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right part: legislature makes, executive implements, judiciary decides breaches
The wrong part: the judiciary also checks laws against the Constitution

questions.q: Compare Fundamental Rights, Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles of State Policy. For each, say whom it addresses and whether a judge can enforce it, and give one example from the chapter's infographic.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights (e.g. Right to Equality, Article 14) are promises to citizens that must be kept: a judge can help someone treated unfairly because of who she is. Fundamental Duties (e.g. to protect and improve the natural environment) are what citizens are expected to follow. Directive Principles (e.g. Article 47 on nutrition) are goals that the government should try to achieve; a judge cannot be asked to enforce them, and they are more like guidelines. The makers wanted some rights to be demanded at once and some bigger goals that might take time.
s: Fundamental Rights: addressee, enforceability, example
Fundamental Duties: addressee and example
Directive Principles: addressee, not enforceable, example

questions.q: Rohan says, 'Article 44 (Uniform Civil Code) carries an Article number in the chapter's infographic, so it is a Fundamental Right I can enforce in court.' What is the best correction?
questions.a: A number does not make a provision a right. The infographic lists Article 44 among the Directive Principles of State Policy, which are goals for the government and cannot be taken to a judge, while the Right against Exploitation is a Fundamental Right even though no number is shown for it.
o: Article 44 is a Directive Principle, a goal for the government that a judge cannot be asked to enforce
Article 44 is a Fundamental Duty, so every citizen must obey it and the court will punish those who do not
Article 44 is a Fundamental Right for citizens who ask the government first, and only then can a judge enforce it
Article 44 is a Fundamental Right, but the infographic shows only the Directive Principles with Article numbers

questions.q: Under the Fundamental Duty about a child's education, a parent must give opportunities from the lower to the upper age limit named in the chapter. Mr. Das enrols his daughter on the day she reaches the lower limit. The duty then covers her for ___ more years.

Assertion (A): Article 21-A makes education a Fundamental Right.
Reason (R): A Fundamental Duty asks a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child between the age of six and fourteen years.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the duty of the parent is a separate provision; it is not the reason why education is a Fundamental Right, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Choose any three Fundamental Duties from the chapter and give one way in which a Class 7 student can follow each.
questions.a: For example: respect the National Flag and National Anthem by standing in attention during assembly; protect the environment by not littering and planting saplings; value heritage by visiting a local monument carefully; strive for excellence in studies and sports.
s: First duty with a realistic way to follow it
Second duty with a way
Third duty with a way

questions.q: True or False: A family refused a rented room because of their caste may ask a court for help, but a group of villagers cannot ask a court to force the government to improve nutrition under Article 47; the makers designed the Constitution with both kinds of provisions on purpose. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. Fundamental Rights are promises that must be kept, so a judge can help someone treated unfairly because of who she is; Directive Principles are goals, not rules a judge can enforce. The makers wanted some rights demanded immediately and some bigger goals that might take time as the country progressed.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: rights are enforceable, DPSP are goals, both created on purpose

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Constitution's key features.
1. A person refused service by a shopkeeper because of who she is can only write to the government, since Fundamental Rights, like the Directive Principles, are guidelines a judge cannot enforce.
2. Article 38 (social, political and economic justice) and Article 47 (nutrition, standard of living and public health) are both among the Directive Principles in the chapter's infographic.
3. The Fundamental Duty about education is addressed to the child, who must stay in school between six and fourteen years of age.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Only statement 2 is from the chapter. Statement 1 is false: Fundamental Rights are promises that must be kept and a judge can help someone treated unfairly because of who she is. Statement 3 is false: the duty is addressed to a parent or guardian, to provide opportunities for education to a child between six and fourteen.

questions.q: A town has two problems: its school turns away girls, and many of its families lack a good standard of living. (a) Which of the two can residents take to a judge now, and which is a 'bigger goal'? (b) What reason does the chapter give for the makers creating both kinds of provisions on purpose?
questions.a: (a) The school turning girls away can be taken to a judge, as it is unfair treatment because of who they are (a Fundamental Right). A good standard of living for all is a Directive Principle, a bigger goal for the government. (b) The makers wanted some rights that could be demanded immediately and some bigger goals that might take time to achieve as the country progressed.
s: Part (a): school matter to a judge; standard of living a bigger goal
Part (b): rights demanded at once, goals that take time as the country progresses

questions.q: Pooja says, 'The Fundamental Duties are printed at the beginning of NCERT textbooks, so they belong to the textbooks and not to the Constitution.' Using the chapter, correct her in two points.
questions.a: The chapter names the Fundamental Duties as a core aspect of the Constitution, alongside the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles. The textbooks only print them in full at the beginning because they are a part of the Constitution.
s: Duties are a core aspect of the Constitution, with Rights and Directive Principles
The textbooks print them in full only because they belong to the Constitution

questions.q:
A Class 7 class in Mysuru makes one quiz card for each item in the chapter's infographic: six Fundamental Duties (a to f), four Fundamental Rights (Equality, Article 14; Freedom, Article 21; Right against Exploitation; Education, Article 21-A) and six Directive Principles (Articles 38, 41, 44, 47, 48-A, 49). The quiz round has time for only 10 of the 16 cards, and the class has agreed to keep at least one card from each of the three groups so that every part of the infographic appears.
(a) What percentage of the 16 cards does each group make up?
(b) Which group is the only one the chapter says a student can demand from a judge, and to whom are the cards of each of the other two groups addressed?
(c) The class must cut 6 cards. Say how many it would cut from each group and justify the split with the chapter. Then name the one card in your cut list that you would most regret losing.
questions.a: (a) Duties 6/16 = 37.5 per cent; Rights 4/16 = 25 per cent; Directive Principles 6/16 = 37.5 per cent. (b) Fundamental Rights are the promises a judge can help with. The Duty cards speak to citizens (for instance a parent or guardian); the Directive Principle cards speak to the government. (c) Any split that leaves at least one card in each group is valid (at most 5 cut from Duties, 3 from Rights, 5 from Directive Principles), with a reason from the chapter. For example, cutting few Rights cards keeps what a student can demand from a judge, and cutting several Directive Principle cards loses part of the social and economic vision the makers had for India, a loss the answer must name.
s: Part (a): 37.5, 25 and 37.5 per cent
Part (b): Rights are demandable from a judge; Duties address citizens, Directive Principles the government
Part (c): a valid split (1), with a chapter reason and the card most regretted (1)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Constitution has laid down an electoral system meant to enable every eligible citizen to vote.
Reason (R): The Constitution lays out the framework of the three organs of government and their roles and responsibilities.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both are true. The chapter states each of them. But R is a separate feature of the Constitution: that it frames the organs does not explain why an electoral system was laid down for every eligible citizen. So R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
Match each situation (Column A) with the part of the Constitution it belongs to (Column B).
Column A: 1. A resident clears litter from the river bank near her house.  2. A court tells a guest house it cannot turn a family away because of their caste.  3. The government opens a nutrition programme in line with Article 47.  4. A girl of nine is admitted to school under Article 21-A.
Column B: a. Fundamental Duty  b. Directive Principle  c. Fundamental Right to equality  d. Fundamental Right to education
questions.a: Clearing litter is the duty to protect the natural environment; the court acts on the Right to Equality; Article 47 is a Directive Principle; Article 21-A is the right to education.

questions.q: A student says, 'India has a two-tier system of government, because the Constitution divides responsibilities only between the central and the state governments.' (a) Correct her using the chapter. (b) What does the chapter say about how responsibilities are shared between the first two tiers?
questions.a: (a) India has a three-tier system of government: central, state and local (the Panchayati Raj system). (b) Some functions and responsibilities are reserved for the central government, and others are assigned to the state government.
s: Part (a): three tiers, naming the local Panchayati Raj tier
Part (b): some functions reserved for the Centre, others assigned to the States

questions.q: Many eligible citizens of a hamlet are left off the voters' list when a Gram Panchayat election is held. (a) Which statement about the electoral system in the chapter does this go against? (b) If the Constitution's design is sound, which organ of government's work is most in question, and why?
questions.a: (a) The Constitution has laid down the electoral system to ensure that every eligible citizen of the country is enabled to vote. (b) The executive, because it implements the law; if the design is sound, the failing lies in carrying it out.
s: Part (a): every eligible citizen must be enabled to vote
Part (b): the executive implements, so the failing lies in carrying it out if the design is sound

questions.q: The chapter says Part IV-A was added in 1976. By then the Constitution, which came into effect in the year that Republic Day marks, had been in effect for ___ years.

The government publishes a proposed rule and invites feedback. A student says, 'Once the public has commented, the rule has to be changed as the public says.' Using the chapter's account of how changes are made to the Constitution, (a) say what the chapter claims about seeking the public's opinion, and (b) say what must still happen before an amendment is accepted.
questions.a: (a) The chapter says opinions are sought from the general public 'many times'; it does not say the public's opinion decides the change. (b) The amendment is rigorously debated in Parliament before it is accepted, and some changes also require a debate in the legislative assemblies.
s: Part (a): opinions are sought many times, but they do not decide the change
Part (b): rigorous debate in Parliament (and, for some, in legislative assemblies)

questions.q: A club writes into its rules: 'These rules shall never be amended, whatever the future brings.' Which statement from the chapter does this rule most directly go against?
o: The makers realised that a need for new laws and rules would emerge over time
Any amendment is rigorously debated in Parliament before it is accepted
Officials pledge to uphold the Constitution and promise to follow its provisions
The text was written by hand and illustrated with scenes from Indian history
questions.a: The chapter calls the Constitution a living document because its makers realised that a need for new laws and rules would emerge over time. A rule that bars all amendment goes against that. Rigorous debate is how amendments are tested, not a bar on them.

questions.q:
The civics club of a Jaipur school plans a wall display titled 'Citizens and the Constitution' with room for two of four entries.
Entry 1: in 2004 a citizen challenged a rule about flying the national flag in court, and the Supreme Court agreed that flying it is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression.
Entry 2: the 73rd Amendment of 1992, which integrated Panchayati Raj.
Entry 3: Part IV-A, added in 1976.
Entry 4: the government's practice of inviting feedback on proposed laws or changes in rules.
The club has two requirements: the display must show an ordinary citizen changing an outcome by going to court, and it must show at least one change to the Constitution's written text.
(a) Which Part was added in 1976, and what is it about?
(b) For which entries does the chapter itself show citizens taking part, and for which does it say nothing about who started the change?
(c) Choose the two entries. Say which requirement each of your entries meets, and why no other pair does as well.
questions.a: (a) Part IV-A, Fundamental Duties. (b) Entries 1 and 4 show citizens taking part (a citizen's challenge in court; public feedback). For Entries 2 and 3 the chapter states the change but not who started it. (c) Entry 1 shows a citizen at work, but it was a court reading of an existing right, so it did not change the written text; the second entry must therefore be Entry 2 or Entry 3 (Panchayati Raj integrated in 1992; Part IV-A added in 1976), which change the text. Entry 4 shows citizens giving feedback but not going to court, so it does not meet the first requirement; the pair 1 and 4 therefore lacks a change to the text, and the pair 2 and 3 lacks a citizen in court. So the pairs 1 and 2, or 1 and 3, are the only ones that meet both requirements.
s: Part (a): Part IV-A, Fundamental Duties
Part (b): Entries 1 and 4 show citizens; for 2 and 3 the chapter is silent on who started the change
Part (c): Entry 1 with Entry 2 or 3 (1), with each requirement matched and the other pairs rejected (1)

questions.q: Naina's grandfather says, 'Our Panchayati Raj came with the Constitution in 1950.' Her teacher corrects him using the chapter's dates, and Naina works out the gap from 1950. Which correction is right?
questions.a: The chapter says Panchayati Raj was not part of the original Constitution; it was integrated in 1992 with the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, which is 1992 - 1950 = 42 years after the Constitution came into effect.
o: Integrated in 1992 through the 73rd Amendment, 42 years after it came into effect
Integrated in 1976 through the 42nd Amendment, 26 years after it came into effect
Integrated in 1992 through the 73rd Amendment, 16 years after it came into effect
Integrated in 2004 by a Supreme Court ruling, 54 years after it came into effect

questions.q: Zoya says, 'Every change to the Constitution since 1950 was started by Parliament, so ordinary citizens can only watch.' Test her claim with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says some changes can be initiated by popular movements, and opinions are sought from the general public before changes are accepted. Parliament debates amendments, but it is not the only starting point, and citizens are not mere spectators.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Popular movements can initiate changes
Opinions of the general public are sought

questions.q: The handwritten original of the Constitution was written and illustrated by named people, and its pages carry scenes such as a gurukula, Akbar with Mughal architecture and Nalanda. (a) Who wrote its text by hand, and who led the team that illustrated its pages? (b) A visitor says, 'The illustrations show only ancient India.' Test her claim using the scenes named here and the range of scenes the chapter gives.
questions.a: (a) Calligrapher Prem Behari Narain Raizada wrote the text by hand; Nandalal Bose and his team illustrated the pages. (b) Her claim is wrong. The chapter says the scenes run from Mohenjo-daro to the freedom movement, so they reach well beyond the earliest times, and the scene with Akbar and Mughal architecture is one that is not from ancient India.
s: Part (a): Raizada for the text; Nandalal Bose and his team for the illustrations
Part (b): claim rejected, using the range from Mohenjo-daro to the freedom movement and the Akbar scene

questions.q: A museum label must show that the Constitution is both 'a living document' and 'a work of art'. Which pair of facts from the chapter does the label need?
o: Part IV-A was added in 1976; a calligrapher wrote its text by hand and its pages show Indian history
Panchayati Raj was integrated in 1992; the Constitution is kept in a helium-filled glass case in Parliament
It has 25 parts and 12 schedules; officials pledge to uphold it and promise to follow its provisions
A calligrapher wrote its text by hand; Nandalal Bose and his team illustrated its pages with scenes
questions.a: 'Living document' needs a fact about change (Part IV-A in 1976 or the 1992 amendment) and 'work of art' needs a fact about the handwriting and illustrations. The option pairing the 1992 amendment with the glass case in Parliament protects the book but is not about art; the option with 25 parts and 12 schedules and the officials' pledge has neither; the option with only the calligrapher and the illustrators supports the art description alone.

questions.q: After the 2004 flag ruling the chapter adds that the tricolour should 'never be dishonoured'. (a) Which Fundamental Duty in the chapter's list does this reminder connect to? (b) Explain how a right and a duty sit together in this example.
questions.a: (a) The duty to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem. (b) The right to freedom of expression lets citizens fly the flag; the duty requires that they respect it and never dishonour it.
s: Part (a): duty to respect the National Flag
Part (b): right to fly it with the duty not to dishonour it

questions.q: A proposal to amend the Constitution is in the news. A residents' group, Nagar Manch, says, 'Only Parliament will see it, and nobody will ever ask us.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: Parliament debates it rigorously, some changes need the assemblies too, and the public is often asked
Parliament debates it rigorously and, in every single case, the public must be asked before it is accepted
Only the legislative assemblies debate it, and Parliament accepts their result without a debate of its own
Parliament may accept it after a quick vote, since the Supreme Court alone examines it afterwards
questions.a: The chapter says changes are rigorously debated in Parliament, some require a debate in legislative assemblies as well, and many times opinions are sought from the general public, so the group is not entirely right. The option that says the public must be asked in every single case turns 'many times' into 'every case'; the option in which only the assemblies debate it, and the option with a quick vote in Parliament and an examination afterwards by the Supreme Court alone, both drop the rigorous debate in Parliament.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Supreme Court's 2004 ruling on flying the national flag changed the written text of the Constitution.
Reason (R): The Court agreed that flying the flag is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter says the Court read an existing Fundamental Right to cover flag flying; it does not say the text was changed. R is true as the chapter states it, and in fact shows why A is wrong.

questions.q:
Read the statements about how the Constitution changes.
1. Part IV-A on Fundamental Duties was added to the Constitution in 1976, after it came into effect.
2. Opinions of the general public are sought on some changes, and some changes need a debate in the legislative assemblies as well as in Parliament.
