3. The Panchayati Raj system was in the original Constitution of 1950 and was only renamed by the 73rd Amendment in 1992.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 is false: Panchayati Raj was not part of the original Constitution and was integrated in it in 1992.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: True or False: The Supreme Court's 2004 ruling on flying the national flag added a new Fundamental Right to the Constitution. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Supreme Court agreed that flying the flag is part of the existing Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression; the court read a right already in the Constitution, and the chapter does not say a new right was added.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the court held that flying the flag falls under the existing Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression

questions.q: A visitor reads that the Constitution had 22 parts when it came into effect and has 25 parts now. (a) What is the net increase in the number of parts? (b) Which one added part does the chapter name, and in which year was it added?
questions.a: (a) 25 - 22 = 3 parts (a net increase; the chapter gives only the totals). (b) Part IV-A, Fundamental Duties, added in 1976.
s: Part (a): net increase of 3
Part (b): Part IV-A (Fundamental Duties), 1976

questions.q: Examine the three developments the chapter describes: Part IV-A (1976), the integration of Panchayati Raj by the 73rd Amendment (1992) and the Supreme Court's flag ruling (2004). For each, say what happened and by what route, and what it shows about the Constitution; then say what the chapter tells us every amendment goes through before it is accepted.
questions.a: Part IV-A: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution, showing that new parts can be added. Panchayati Raj: not in the original Constitution, it was integrated in 1992 by the 73rd Amendment, showing the Constitution can take in structures the country needs. Flag ruling: a citizen challenged a rule in court and the Supreme Court said flying the flag is part of the Fundamental Right to Freedom of Expression, showing that a citizen's challenge can change how a right is read, though the chapter does not call it an amendment. Every amendment is rigorously debated in Parliament before it is accepted; some also need a debate in the legislative assemblies, and opinions are often sought from the public.
s: Part IV-A with route and lesson
Panchayati Raj with route and lesson
Flag ruling as a court reading of an existing right, with lesson
Amendments: rigorous debate in Parliament
Legislative assemblies for some changes and public opinion

questions.q: A Class 7 council wants to change one rule in its own class constitution. Borrowing from how the chapter says the national Constitution is changed, write a three-step procedure for the council and say which of the chapter's features each step copies.
questions.a: Any workable procedure, e.g. (1) the proposed change is debated rigorously by the council, copying the debate in Parliament; (2) it is also debated by the section representatives, copying the legislative assemblies; (3) classmates' opinions are sought before it is accepted, copying the public feedback.
s: A three-step procedure that could work
Steps linked to debate by the main body and the wider assemblies
A step that seeks the opinion of those affected

questions.q: 'A good constitution should be easy to change.' Evaluate this statement using the chapter's account of how the Indian Constitution is changed and why the makers allowed change.
questions.a: For: the makers realised a need for new laws and rules would emerge, so Part IV-A (1976) and Panchayati Raj (1992) could be added and the Constitution is a living document that can be improved as needs change. Against: every change is rigorously debated in Parliament, some need debate in the legislative assemblies too, and the public is consulted, so change is deliberately careful. Judgement: the chapter supports a Constitution that can change, but not one that changes easily; a good balance is change after wide debate.
s: Reason for allowing change with two examples
Safeguards: debate, assemblies, public opinion
A balanced judgement

questions.q: Arrange these in the order they took place and say what each shows: (i) the Supreme Court's flag ruling, (ii) the 73rd Amendment on Panchayati Raj, (iii) the addition of Part IV-A. How many years separate the earliest and the latest of the three?
questions.a: Order: Part IV-A (1976), Panchayati Raj (1992), flag ruling (2004). Part IV-A and Panchayati Raj are additions by amendment; the flag ruling shows a court interpreting a right. 2004 - 1976 = 28 years.
s: Correct order with years
What each shows (amendments and court interpretation)
28 years

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The 73rd Amendment shows that the Constitution can take in a structure that its original text did not have.
Reason (R): The 73rd Amendment was passed 26 years after Part IV-A was added.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true: Panchayati Raj was integrated in 1992 with the 73rd Amendment and was not part of the original Constitution. R is false: Part IV-A was added in 1976, and 1992 - 1976 = 16 years, not 26.

questions.q:
Sky Guild, an online game group of 240 members, has two proposed rule changes. Change X: a rise in every member's monthly fee. Change Y: a ban on a game that 30 of the 240 members play. The guild can run its slow process (Plan 2) for only one of them this month; the other goes through the quick one (Plan 1).
Plan 1: the five-member admin council votes next Sunday.
Plan 2: the council posts the draft for two weeks for comments, the whole guild debates and votes, and if 40 members sign a petition the council must also put the signatories' proposal to the guild.
(a) Which two features of the Constitution's way of changing do the posted-draft comments and the whole guild's debate copy?
(b) What percentage of the guild must sign the petition, and what percentage do the 30 players of the game make up? Can the 30 players trigger the petition on their own?
(c) Which change should get Plan 2? Choose, and say what the supporters or opponents of the other change can still do, using what the chapter says about how changes begin.
questions.a: (a) Public feedback on proposed changes (opinions sought from the general public) and debate in a wider body, like the legislative assemblies after Parliament. (b) 40/240 = 16.7 per cent are needed; 30/240 = 12.5 per cent are players, so they are 10 members short and cannot trigger the petition alone. (c) Either can be defended. Change X touches all 240 members, which fits the rigorous debate and public opinion the chapter stresses. Change Y affects a group too small to start the petition, so Plan 2's open debate is the only place where it is heard. For the change put through Plan 1, the chapter says some changes can be initiated by popular movements, so those who disagree can organise and press the council.
s: Part (a): public feedback and debate in a wider body
Part (b): 16.7 per cent against 12.5 per cent; the players cannot trigger the petition alone
Part (c): a decision with a chapter-based reason (1), and what the other side can still do (1)

questions.q: A student may think what she likes about a school rule but is stopped from writing about it in the school magazine. (a) Under Liberty the chapter lists three areas of freedom; which one is being restricted here? (b) Does the Preamble's wording say that no restriction at all can ever be placed on expression? Explain.
questions.a: (a) How she wishes to express her thoughts. (b) No: the chapter says there are no unreasonable restrictions, so it rules out unreasonable restrictions, not every restriction.
s: Part (a): the area of expressing thoughts
Part (b): only unreasonable restrictions are ruled out

questions.q: The chapter says the core values are present across the Constitution, but their essence is written in the Preamble. In the chapter's infographic, name the Preamble word that is closest in meaning to (a) Article 14 (equality before law) and (b) Article 38 (social, political and economic justice), and quote or paraphrase the Preamble's own explanation of each word.
questions.a: (a) Equality: the Preamble says all are equal before the law. (b) Justice, the closest word: the Preamble says citizens cannot be discriminated against, social inequalities are to be reduced and the government should work for the welfare of all, especially of less advantaged groups.
s: Part (a): Equality, with 'all are equal before the law'
Part (b): Justice, with its explanation

questions.q: True or False: A country whose head of state is chosen by an elected assembly, and not by a direct vote of every citizen, can still be a Republic in the Preamble's sense, provided the post is not hereditary. Give a reason for your verdict.
questions.a: True. The chapter's test for a Republic is that the head of the state is an elected person and not a hereditary position. It does not say that every citizen must vote for the head directly, so election by an elected assembly passes the test as long as the post does not go by birth.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the test is that the head is elected and not hereditary; a direct vote by every citizen is not what the chapter requires

questions.q: A school adopts two rules. Rule 1: 'No senior may speak of a junior as lesser, whatever the junior's background.' Rule 2: 'The principal shall ensure that every student has the same chance to join every team.' (a) Name the Preamble value each rule reflects. (b) Which of the two depends mainly on how students behave towards one another, and which on what the authority provides? Use the chapter's wording.
questions.a: (a) Rule 1 reflects Fraternity (no one should treat a fellow citizen as inferior); Rule 2 reflects Equality (the government should ensure equal opportunity for all). (b) Fraternity depends on how citizens behave towards one another, 'as if members of the same family'; Equality depends on what the authority ensures.
s: Part (a): Fraternity for Rule 1, Equality for Rule 2
Part (b): Fraternity from behaviour, Equality from what the authority ensures

questions.q:
A district in Assam has money for only one of two steps this year. Step 1: a limit on how much farmland a single large estate may own. Step 2: scholarships for children from the less advantaged families of the district. A critic says, 'Scholarships treat students unequally because only some get them, so they go against the Preamble's Equality.' A supporter says, 'Step 1 matters more because it stops the problem at its root.'
(a) Which Preamble value does Step 1 show, what does the chapter say the government may regulate under it, and was this word in the Preamble at the start?
(b) The chapter's explanation of Equality includes two ideas: that all are equal before the law, and that the government should ensure equal opportunity for all. Which of the two does the critic's objection rest on, and which does Step 2 serve?
(c) Evaluate the critic's objection, then choose which step to fund. Name the Preamble word your choice serves most directly.
questions.a: (a) Socialist; the government should regulate the ownership of land and industry to reduce socio-economic inequalities; the word was added in 1976 (42nd Amendment), so it was not in the Preamble at the start. (b) The objection treats every student exactly alike, which stretches 'equal before the law' to cover who gets a benefit; Step 2 serves equal opportunity for all, and also Justice, which includes the welfare of less advantaged groups. (c) The objection is weak: the chapter's Equality asks the government to ensure equal opportunity and to end social inequalities, which scholarships for the less advantaged serve. Either step can then be chosen: Step 1 serves Socialist (reducing socio-economic inequalities); Step 2 serves Justice (welfare of less advantaged groups) and equal opportunity. Marks go for the objection tested against the chapter's two ideas and a choice tied to a named Preamble word.
s: Part (a): Socialist; regulating ownership of land and industry; added in 1976
Part (b): the objection rests on equality before the law; Step 2 serves equal opportunity (and Justice)
Part (c): objection tested (1), choice tied to a named Preamble word (1)

questions.q: A poster lists nine value words of the Preamble: sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic, republic, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity. Going by the chapter's note on the 42nd Amendment, the number of these nine that were already in the Preamble before 1976 is ___.

Assertion (A): A State law limiting how much farmland any one owner may hold is consistent with the Preamble's description of 'Socialist'.
Reason (R): Justice, as the Preamble explains it, includes the government working for the welfare of less advantaged groups.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, but R does not explain A. A rests on the chapter's own description of Socialist: the government should regulate the ownership of land and industry to reduce socio-economic inequalities. R is a true statement about Justice, a different Preamble word.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A small country's rulers are elected, and its constitution was drawn up by the people's representatives. But an ambassador of a neighbouring power must approve every major law before it comes into force. Which of the Preamble words, as the chapter explains them, does this country fail to meet?
questions.a: Sovereign means the people have the supreme right to decide internal and external matters and no external power can dictate to the government. A neighbour's approval of laws is such dictation. The elected rulers satisfy Democratic and the people's own constitution satisfies 'We, the People'.
o: Sovereign
Democratic
Republic
Secular

questions.q:
A district federation of sports clubs will name one club's way of running itself as a model for clubs that want to follow the Preamble's values.
Club A: members elect the chair each year and ask her for accounts, but a rule forbids members from speaking against the committee's plans at meetings.
Club B: the chair's post passes from parent to child; she gives public accounts every year and members may speak openly at meetings.
Club C: members elect the chair each year, ask for accounts and speak openly, but members of one caste are not allowed to hold any post.
(a) For each club, name the Preamble word its flaw goes against and give the chapter's meaning of that word.
(b) Which club's flaw lies in how its head is chosen?
(c) Rank the three clubs from best to worst model for the federation. Justify the club you put last, using the chapter's wording.
questions.a: (a) Club A: Liberty (no unreasonable restrictions on how citizens express their thoughts). Club B: Republic (the head of the state is an elected person and not a hereditary position). Club C: Justice (citizens cannot be discriminated against on grounds of caste, religion and gender). (b) Club B. (c) Any ranking is acceptable if the last place is justified from the chapter's wording; for example, Club B last because its post goes by birth, which is the exact thing a Republic rules out, even though it keeps accounts and free speech. The chapter does not rank the values, so the answer must argue from the meanings.
s: Part (a): Liberty, Republic and Justice matched with their meanings
Part (b): Club B
Part (c): a ranking (1), with the last place justified from the chapter's wording (1)

questions.q: A new government school lists these features: (i) admission is open to children of every caste, religion and gender; (ii) there is no official prayer and students keep their own festivals without asking permission; (iii) the students' council is elected each year and must present its accounts to the students; (iv) students are told they may not write or speak on any rule of the school, even politely; (v) a minister's child and a clerk's child who break the same school rule face the same consequence. Name the Preamble value reflected in (i) (judged by the Preamble's wording on discrimination), (ii), (iii) and (v) (judged by its wording on all being equal before the law) with a reason, and say which feature goes against a Preamble value, which one, and what change you would suggest.
questions.a: (i) Justice: citizens cannot be discriminated against on grounds of caste, religion and gender. (Equal opportunity for all is also in the chapter's Equality, but the wording on discrimination is Justice's.) (ii) Secular: no official religion and freedom to follow any faith. (iii) Democratic: rulers are elected and held accountable. (v) Equality: all are equal before the law (rule). (iv) goes against Liberty: there should be no unreasonable restrictions on how citizens express their thoughts; students should be allowed to put forward views on school rules politely.
s: Justice for (i) with reason
Secular for (ii) with reason
Democratic for (iii) with reason
Equality for (v) with reason
(iv) against Liberty with a suggested change

questions.q: A government announces: 'We will treat all religions with equal respect, and from next year one religion will be the official religion of the State.' Using the Preamble's meaning of Secular, show why the two parts of the announcement cannot both hold.
questions.a: Secular means citizens have complete freedom to follow any religion, but there is no official religion, and the government treats all beliefs and practices with equal respect. Naming one religion the official religion of the State breaks the 'no official religion' part and therefore the 'equal respect' part too, so the two promises contradict each other.
s: States the chapter's meaning: no official religion, equal respect
Shows an official religion contradicts equal respect
Concludes the two cannot both be true

questions.q:
Match each situation (Column A) with the Preamble word it shows (Column B).
Column A: 1. A school has no official prayer, and students keep their own festivals without seeking anyone's permission.  2. A State limits how much farmland and industry one owner can hold.  3. Pupils of every caste and both genders share the same classroom benches and the same well.  4. A foreign embassy asks to approve a country's laws, and the government refuses.
Column B: a. Sovereign  b. Secular  c. Justice  d. Socialist
questions.a: No official religion with freedom of practice is Secular; regulating ownership of land and industry is Socialist; no discrimination on caste or gender is Justice; refusing outside dictation is Sovereign.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): 'Secular' means the State must discourage religious practice so that all citizens are treated alike.
Reason (R): Under 'Secular', citizens have complete freedom to follow any religion.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false: the chapter says there is no official religion and the government treats all beliefs and practices with equal respect; it does not ask the State to discourage any. R is true as the chapter states it, and shows why A is wrong.

questions.q: A country's constitution opens: 'We, the Subjects of King X, accept this Constitution given to us by His Majesty, whose son will rule after him.' (a) Which phrase of India's Preamble does this opening go against, and what does the chapter say that phrase means? (b) Which Preamble word does the hereditary succession go against?
questions.a: (a) 'We, the People of India': the chapter says the Constitution has been drawn up and enacted by the people through their representatives, and not handed down to them by a king or any outside powers. (b) Republic: the head of the state is an elected person and not a hereditary position.
s: Part (a): 'We, the People'; drawn up by the people, not handed down by a king
Part (b): Republic; head of state not hereditary

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Preamble.
1. A Republic is a country with no head of state at all, since the people govern directly through the Constitution.
2. 'Secular' means the State treats every religion with equal respect, so it must encourage every citizen to follow a religion.
3. 'Socialist' means wealth is generated socially and should be shared, and the government should regulate the ownership of land and industry to reduce socio-economic inequalities.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
o: 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
questions.a: Only statement 3 is from the chapter. Statement 1 is false: a Republic has a head of state who is an elected person and not a hereditary one. Statement 2 is false: Secular means complete freedom to follow any religion, with no official religion; it does not require anyone to follow one.

questions.q: Three countries are described. P: its head of state and assembly are elected, but a foreign government must approve every major law. Q: its government decides all matters itself, and the people elect an assembly that holds the ministers accountable, but the head of state is a king whose son will succeed him. R: its government decides all matters itself and its head of state is elected for five years, but the assembly was appointed by the head of state and answers to no one. For each country, name the word among Sovereign, Democratic and Republic that is not met, and give the chapter's meaning of that word. Then say in two sentences how the three words together answer the question 'who governs India?'
questions.a: P fails Sovereign: the people have the supreme right to decide internal and external matters and no external power can dictate to the government. Q fails Republic: the head of the state is an elected person and not a hereditary position. R fails Democratic: the people elect their rulers and hold them accountable. Together the three words describe a country whose government is independent of outside powers (Sovereign), chosen by its people and answerable to them (Democratic) and headed by an elected, non-hereditary head (Republic), so the people govern India.
s: P: Sovereign with its meaning

questions.q: Tara says, 'The Preamble says Socialist, so the government must take over all land and industry and no one may own any.' Test her claim against the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter explains Socialist as wealth being generated socially and shared by society, and says the government should regulate the ownership of land and industry to reduce socio-economic inequalities. Regulating ownership is not the same as abolishing it, and the chapter does not say that no one may own anything.
s: Verdict: disagrees
States the chapter's meaning of Socialist
Regulate versus take over or abolish

questions.q: In a town, the mayor is chosen each year by a lottery among the town's families, and she need not explain her spending to anyone. Which idea in the Preamble's description of 'Democratic' is missing?
questions.a: Democratic means the people enjoy equal political rights, elect their rulers and hold them accountable. A lottery means the people do not elect the ruler, and the mayor does not answer to the people, so the central ideas of electing rulers and holding them accountable are both absent.
o: The people elect their rulers and hold them accountable
The head of state is an elected person and not a hereditary one
No external power can dictate to the government
There is no official religion and every faith is treated with equal respect

questions.q: A critic says four arrangements all fail the Preamble's Equality. Which one really does fail it, as the chapter explains Equality?
o: A library lets the chairman's relatives keep books for a year while others get two weeks
A school gives extra coaching to children from poorer homes who are struggling in studies
A scholarship notice invites applications only from families below a stated income limit
Every applicant sits the same paper in an entrance test held on the same day for all
questions.a: Equality means all are equal before the law (the rules) and the government should ensure equal opportunity for all. Giving the chairman's relatives a privilege that other members do not have breaks equality before the rules. Extra help for poorer children and an income-limited scholarship are ways of working for the welfare of less advantaged groups, which the chapter includes in Justice, and the same paper for everyone is equal opportunity.
